passage:
At the park in Osaka, a smiling woman on a bench held out a pink sweet. "Want one?" Yuki, five, trotted toward her at once.
"Yuki, come back to me," called Aiko, his mother, catching his hand. "We don't take sweets from people we don't know." The woman nodded and put it away.
Later the wind blew Yuki's hat under a hedge. A tall park keeper in a grey coat, face serious, pulled it out and held it up. Yuki hid behind Aiko's legs.
"He works here, see his badge?" Aiko said softly. Yuki peeked, grabbed the hat and whispered, "Thank you."

qa.q: What did the woman on the bench hold out?
qa.a: A pink sweet.

qa.q: Why did Yuki trot toward the smiling woman but hide from the park keeper?
qa.a: The smile and the pink sweet felt nice, so she seemed safe, while the keeper's serious face made Yuki nervous, even though he was the one helping.

qa.q: What rule did Aiko use, and why does it suit a five-year-old?
qa.a: We don't take sweets from people we don't know; a simple rule protects Yuki when a nice feeling might make him trust too quickly.

qa.q: How might the park keeper feel when Yuki hides?
qa.a: He might feel a little sad, or be used to it, and glad when Yuki finally whispers thank you.

grounding: A five-year-old heads straight for a smiling stranger with a sweet but hides from a serious-looking park keeper who is helping him.

passage:
In the kindergarten garden, Vikas spotted shiny red berries on a hedge. "Sweets!" he said, and reached out.
"Stop, Vikas." Miss Fernandes knelt beside him. "Those aren't for eating. We only eat food from our tiffin or from grown-ups we know."
Near the gate, Deepak Bhaiya, the school caretaker with a big moustache and a mop, bent down. "Your lace is open, little one."
Vikas scrunched his face and ran back to Miss Fernandes, clutching her dupatta.
"That's Deepak Bhaiya. He helps us every day," she said. "Shall we let him tie it together?"
Vikas held her hand tight and stuck out one foot.

qa.q: What did Vikas spot on the hedge?
qa.a: Shiny red berries.

qa.q: Why did the berries seem good to Vikas but Deepak Bhaiya seem scary?
qa.a: The berries looked like sweets, so they felt nice and safe, while the big moustache and mop made him nervous, though Deepak Bhaiya only wanted to help.

qa.q: How did Miss Fernandes handle each of Vikas's feelings?
qa.a: She stopped the berries with a clear rule, and with the caretaker she named him and stayed close so Vikas could accept help while feeling safe.

qa.q: What might Deepak Bhaiya think when Vikas runs away?
qa.a: He may feel a little hurt, or be used to it, and patient enough to wait while the teacher introduces him.

grounding: A kindergarten child reaches for sweet-looking berries but runs from a kind caretaker, because nice and nervous feelings decide what seems safe.

passage:
I'm Irfan, and on Sunday I took my little brother Abhinav to the fair with Ammi.
A man in a sparkly hat was giving out free candyfloss near the back gate. Abhinav let go of my hand and ran straight to him. I caught up and pulled him back to Ammi.
Later he got lost for a minute near the swings. A lady at the help desk, in a plain brown sweater, knelt and asked his name. Abhinav screamed and wouldn't answer until Ammi came running.
I don't know exactly what he was thinking. Maybe sparkly felt friendly and plain felt scary. Now we practise who to ask for help.

qa.q: What was the man near the back gate giving out?
qa.a: Free candyfloss.

qa.q: What might explain why Abhinav ran to one stranger but screamed at the other?
qa.a: The sparkly hat and candyfloss probably felt fun and friendly, while the plain helper felt strange and scary, so his feelings decided who seemed safe.

qa.q: What could Ammi and Irfan practise with Abhinav?
qa.a: Staying with the grown-up he came with, and if he is lost, going to a help desk or staff member instead of whoever looks fun.

qa.q: How did Irfan probably feel when Abhinav let go and ran?
qa.a: A jolt of worry and responsibility, which is why Irfan ran to catch up and bring Abhinav back to Ammi.

grounding: An older sibling sees a young child run to a sparkly stranger with candyfloss yet scream at a plainly dressed help-desk worker.

passage:
Tuesday: At the colony park, a smiling man held out a pink lollipop. Tenzin, five, ran straight to him. His aunt Nirmala hurried over and took his hand. "We don't take sweets from people we don't know." Tenzin pouted. "But he smiled."
Thursday: The new bus helper, a tall aunty with a plain grey sari and no smile, reached for his bag. Tenzin hid behind Nirmala and cried.
Next Monday: The same helper knelt and tied his loose shoelace. Tenzin peeked at her, then held out his hand to climb in.

qa.q: What did the smiling man hold out to Tenzin?
qa.a: A pink lollipop.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin cry when the bus helper reached for his bag?
qa.a: Tenzin felt scared because she looked plain and did not smile, even though she was there to help.

qa.q: What did Nirmala do well when Tenzin ran to the stranger?
qa.a: She hurried over, took his hand and calmly said they don't take sweets from people they don't know.

qa.q: How might the bus helper feel when Tenzin hides from her?
qa.a: She might feel a little sad or patient, knowing children need time, which is why she knelt to tie his shoelace later.

grounding: Over several days a young boy trusts a smiling stranger and fears a plain-looking helper, guided by how each makes him feel.

passage: The Kolkata station was packed and noisy, and Papa, Manoj, was stuck in a long ticket queue. Siddharth, five, held the bag strap. A man with a shiny red balloon bent down, smiling. "Want to see the big engine?" Siddharth let go of the strap. Papa turned just then, dropped out of the queue, and scooped him up. "We stay together. Always." Later a lady from the help desk, in a plain blue uniform, came to check on them. Siddharth buried his face in Papa's shirt and would not look at her.

qa.q: What did the man with the balloon ask Siddharth?
qa.a: "Want to see the big engine?"

qa.q: Why did Siddharth let go of the bag strap?
qa.a: The shiny balloon and the smiling man felt nice and exciting, so Siddharth felt safe going with him.

qa.q: What choice did Papa make when he saw the man, and why was it right?
qa.a: He left the queue at once and picked Siddharth up, because staying together mattered more than the tickets.

qa.q: How might the help-desk lady feel when Siddharth hides from her?
qa.a: She may understand that he's scared and tired, even though she came to help, and keep her distance kindly.

grounding: At a crowded station a young boy is drawn to a smiling stranger and hides from a plain-looking helper, judging by feelings.
